  "body": "The selected account poses this as a problem of agreement technology: agreements are underspecified, schedules decay them, avoidance blocks the venue where they would be repaired, so it proposes better ways to make, record and renew agreements. There is another pose available. Ask not how this household can make better agreements, but why it needs so many.

Start with a structural fact the first account touches only at its limit — formalization 'reads as contract enforcement between friends' — but does not put at the centre: between friends, agreements cannot be enforced. The sanctions actually available — confrontation, withdrawal — cost the enforcer about as much as the offender, so friendship blocks the machinery that makes explicit obligations cheap elsewhere. Every chore agreement therefore adds a claim that must be remembered and interpreted while adding no cheap way to settle it. A household that governs itself through many small agreements is accumulating a stock of unenforceable claims, and 'we disagree about what the agreement meant' is simply what that stock produces when drawn on. On this pose, the first move is not to clarify the agreements but to reduce how many exist.

Five moves follow, roughly in decreasing order of confidence.

1. Shrink the coordination surface before clarifying it. Some contested obligations can be dissolved rather than assigned: fewer shared possessions, each person's own food arrangements where feasible, a tool that deletes a task. Eliminating an obligation takes it out of dispute permanently; clarifying one leaves it a site of interpretation, and interpretation disputes tend to reopen wearing new words. The practical form is a single inventory conversation — everything the household currently treats as shared, each item marked keep, clarify or eliminate. Nothing here says most items can go; a flat's kitchen is probably irreducible. The claim is about direction: the first account tightens the agreement system; this loosens the load on it.

2. Where spillover is low, replace negotiation with ownership. Divide by domain rather than task: one person owns the bathroom outright, including the standard and the timing, and the owner's word settles disputes inside the domain because the owner is the standard's author. Ownership also absorbs schedule change better than a split — the owner flexes within the zone rather than renegotiating — which addresses the decay problem without a renewal meeting. The costs are real and should be said: domains are unequal, boundaries leak, a lax owner imposes at the edges. This is a tool for low-spillover areas, not a constitution.

3. Test the manager hypothesis. The description has a signature: it is written from the position of someone who tracks what was agreed, notices non-performance and initiates the conversations — the household's de facto manager. If that role is real, three things follow. The meaning-disputes may be disputes between a manager and the managed. The avoidance may be avoidance not of chores but of the follow-up energy itself — the first account raises this as a caution; here it is the primary hypothesis. And there is an invisible workload — noticing, remembering, chasing — that appears in no agreement, which the asker may be over-carrying or over-wielding; both readings fit the description and they demand opposite responses. A bounded experiment separates them: an announced, not silent, two-week stop on initiating and following up. Watch who steps up, what degrades, what the others say. Either finding is useful — evidence of dependence is a grievance worth naming out loud; evidence that the follow-ups generate the friction is a reason to change role, not wording. The announcement is mandatory because a silent stop reads as a strike.

4. Fix the default rule for unclaimed work. Households like this often run on an unstated rule: what nobody does falls to whoever is most bothered. If that rule is operating, avoidance is being paid — the disengaged friend is not failing the system; the system is working — and no written agreement survives it, because the note-keeper becomes the residual doer by another name. Whatever else is adopted, make the unclaimed-task default explicit: within hygiene limits, unclaimed work goes undone, visibly, and the household absorbs the consequence rather than the most-concerned resident absorbing the task.

5. On the avoiding friend: change the medium before the message. The aversive object may be the conversation format itself rather than its content, so before coaxing them back into any conversation, group or one-on-one, try a channel with no face and no moment — a shared list tasks are claimed from asynchronously. The risk is silent non-participation, which is exactly why the unclaimed-task default must be fixed first; an async channel with the old default just routes the work to the asker by a new path.

The two poses make different predictions, which is convenient for the asker. If agreement technology is the right frame, doer-worded written agreements should visibly reduce dispute frequency within a few weeks. If coordination load and role are the right frame, disputes will migrate rather than vanish — from 'what did we agree' to 'you're keeping score', or to enforcement of the notes — because the grievance is about standing, not wording. The cheap way to find out which flat this is: run the first account's cheapest unilateral measure first, and watch what the disputes become.

And the caution crosses accounts unchanged: everything above, including the manager hypothesis, rests on one participant's description, and the first test of any of it remains asking the other two what they think the problem is.",

Work on the problem using the material actually exposed in this request and your background knowledge. The problem has no supplied answer key or scoring rule. Claims, criticisms and methods are fallible. Do not invent a source, an observation, an earlier event, or a dependency to fill a field. A missing view says what you can currently see; it does not establish what happened earlier. Return a JSON object with exactly two independently authored string fields: body and commitments. Body is your public prose contribution. Commitments says what taking your contribution up would involve. An empty commitment surface is allowed when none can be identified. Do not repeat the body wholesale into commitments.

Use FCL-1 for the commitment surface, encoded as a JSON document inside the commitments string: {"language":"FCL-1","records":[...],"uptake":[...]}. Each record has unique local id, type (claim|commitment|objection|use|problem), and text (unrestricted prose). Optional prose fields: scope, action, consequence, grounds, bearing. Optional arrays of references: target, depends, mentions, revises, withdraws. References are local IDs or exposed-artifact-label#local-ID; do not invent hidden IDs. A commitment proposes a scoped use, action, application or consequence; an objection alleges a defect whose bearing can itself be criticized; a use proposes an uptake or response; a problem states an unresolved question. depends asserts reliance; mentions only locates material. uptake lists the records you currently propose to use, not certified truths. No record type or optional field must be present. Empty records and uptake are allowed. Express uncertainty or an unrepresentable relation in prose rather than inventing a relation. The body remains unrestricted prose.

Return one JSON object with exactly two string fields: "body" and "commitments". Write the actual commitments separately; do not copy the body into that field as a storage shortcut.

# rival

Explore another way of posing or addressing the problem. You see the account's body; its commitment field is not supplied.

## Original problem (task)
[01274f41553299e7] (h005.task.v1)
I share a flat with two friends. We keep arguing about ordinary household chores. Sometimes we agree on who will do something, but later we disagree about what the agreement meant. Our work schedules change, and one friend has started avoiding the conversations. What should I do?

## Selected input account (p.rival.0)

BODY
No prior account is available to build on — the selected previous view is absent — so this begins from the asker's description alone, which is itself worth flagging: everything below inherits one participant's angle on a three-person situation.

Three features of the description seem to do most of the explanatory work, and they are not one problem.

First, the disputes are about what an agreement meant, not about whether a task was done. That points at underspecification rather than bad faith: an agreement like 'you take the bins' leaves frequency, standard and deadline open, and each person later reads the gap in their own favor. If that is right, more argument about the past is the wrong tool; what is missing is a way of fixing terms at the moment an agreement is made.

Second, the schedules change, so any fixed split decays. An allocation that was fair in March is unfair by May without anyone misbehaving. A one-time settlement cannot hold; what is needed is a renewal mechanism — which suggests a short, boring, calendarised check-in rather than episodic negotiations that each carry the full weight of accumulated grievance.

Third, the friend who has started avoiding the conversations is the least knowable part and probably the most important. Avoidance of a recurring conversation is usually maintained by the conversation being aversive, and a conversation dominated by retrospective dispute is predictably aversive. There is also a structural suspect: in a three-person household, a group conversation about chores can take on a two-on-one character for whichever resident is least aligned with the other two, so that it feels like judgment rather than planning. But two opposite explanations of the avoidance fit the material — the friend feels unfairly blamed or outnumbered, or the friend is dodging obligations they know they are not meeting — and these call for different responses. The asker cannot tell them apart from inside their own framing, and neither can this account.

One caution the account should carry: it is entirely consistent with the description that the friends experience the asker as relitigating past agreements with prosecutorial energy, and that the avoidance is partly a response to that. The first test of any remedy is whether it survives asking the other two what they think the problem is.

With that in place, what seems worth conjecturing, in decreasing order of confidence:

1. Doer-worded written agreements. When someone agrees to a task, they write down in a shared note or group chat what they agreed to, in their own words, with a frequency or deadline. The doer's own words matter: it is much harder to later dispute the meaning of a sentence you wrote yourself. The asker can start unilaterally with their own undertakings.

2. A recurring short check-in — fifteen minutes, fortnightly — with a fixed agenda: what did not work since last time, and what needs adjusting given the coming period's schedules. Its function is to move disputes off the trigger path: an argument about the bins at the moment the bins are full becomes a scheduled item instead, and schedule drift gets a standing venue.

3. One-on-one, low-stakes contact with the avoiding friend, framed as a question — what would make this easier for you? — rather than as a summons back into the group conversation. Forcing the group format on someone already avoiding it is likely to deepen the avoidance, and it forfeits the chance to learn which explanation of the avoidance is true.

4. A limit rather than a recommendation: how far to formalize (rotas, standards, apps) is constrained by the fact that these are friends. Some explicitness reduces friction; past some point it reads as contract enforcement between friends. Where that line sits is household-specific and will have to be found by trying the light measures first and watching how they land.

The order of operations matters: reduce the aversiveness and ambiguity of coordination first, then ask what the avoider actually needs. The chore disputes look tractable with format changes; the avoidance does not, because its causes are so far only conjectured.

## What to return
A JSON object carrying "body" and "commitments". Both are strings and nothing else is required.
